source.title: Unlocking the Theory Behind Scaling 1-Bit Neural Networks
source.authors: Majid Daliri; Zhao Song; Chiwun Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some displayed equations and theorem statements appear inconsistent or malformed, noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies scaling in 1-bit networks and toy supervised function-learning tasks, extending scaling-law claims to a different training and model setting. It does not test language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical and experimental results on quadratic training loss for 1-bit networks and toy-function MLPs. It does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The FP32 comparisons are comparators, not separate evidence for the original language-model claim.
record.test_reason: The paper calls its results a scaling law for 1-bit networks, but neither result measures the construct in any version. The 'law' (Prop. 4.3) is an NTK convergence upper bound, not a measured loss curve. Its compute term is exponential, not a power law. The experiments report minimum training loss for MLPs fit to 100 synthetic points, at three sizes (2^17, 2^19, 2^21), shown only in figures. No power law is fitted, no exponents are given, and data and compute are never varied. This is an overparameterised memorisation regime, so it cannot show whether the power-law form holds in a new regime (V5) or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors also claim that 1-bit networks match full-precision outputs on train and test inputs as width grows ('generalization similarity'). They also say the 1-bit vs FP32 loss gap shrinks with parameter count. They present this as theory confirming a scaling law for 1-bit networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an NTK-based theoretical analysis of 1-bit two-layer networks and synthetic function-approximation experiments with quadratic loss. It does not use the language-model pretraining, held-out cross-entropy, or allocation-sweep procedure of the original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical conclusions rely on the stated positive-definite NTK assumption and choices of width, learning rate, training duration, and scale coefficient κ. Experiments vary target function, MLP depth, precision comparator, and parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: For MLPs fit to 100 synthetic points, minimum training loss decreases as parameter count grows (2^17 to 2^21), for both 1-bit and FP32 weights. The 1-bit vs FP32 gap is said to shrink with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterised 1-bit (sign-quantised, STE-trained) networks reach training loss comparable to full precision as width grows.

fits_no_version.finding: An NTK-regime bound shows that 1-bit two-layer networks converge to arbitrarily small training loss given large enough width. The bound decays exponentially in compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical convergence guarantee for wide 1-bit networks (NTK regime), not an empirical scaling law.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger 2-layer MLPs reach lower final train and test loss on 1-D functions, with a small train-test gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalisation similarity between train and test fit for wide MLPs on toy 1-D regression.

record.problems: The empirical scaling evidence is for synthetic function learning with quadratic loss, not language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy. The plotted sweeps provide no reported fitted exponents, numerical loss values, or empirical uncertainty estimates. The theoretical scaling proposition has an exponential compute term, not a power-law compute term. The paper's Theorem 5.2 displays a prediction difference comparing f with itself in the informal statement, while the appendix compares the 1-bit and full-precision functions; several displayed equations and theorem statements also appear malformed or inconsistent.
record.rows_left_out: Section 6.2 and Figure 2 compare fitted outputs on three one-dimensional functions at a fixed 20M-parameter setting; these do not report a size-scaling result. Other formal convergence and function-similarity bounds were not added as separate rows because they do not report additional scaling-loss measurements.

untested.parts: Whether a power-law form (fitted exponent over orders of magnitude) holds for 1-bit or quantised training. Only monotone decrease of training loss across three sizes is shown.
Not addressed. Depth 3 vs 5 is shown but not at matched parameter counts, and no comparison is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 'supports' labels are not justified. The 'scaling law' is a convergence upper bound, and the experiments show only monotone training-loss decrease on 100-point toy datasets, with no power-law fit. The bound is exponential in compute, and the theorem statements contain inconsistencies (Theorem 5.2 compares f with itself). This is better treated as using the 'scaling law' label loosely than as a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy in language models, and power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or comparison of how optimal parameter and token counts scale with compute.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or architecture at a fixed parameter count to estimate their effects on loss.
The tested setting is 1-bit networks trained on synthetic supervised function-learning tasks. It does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream language-model tasks or downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.
The paper does not compare alternative fitting choices or setups to show that exponents or compute-optimal allocations change, or that curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: 1-bit two-layer linear network (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives a training-loss relation in parameter count, dataset size, and compute from a convergence theorem.
rows.measure: Theoretical scaling relation for training loss
rows.uncertainty: Theorem statements include probability at least 1 − δ; δ ∈ (0, 0.1).
rows.note: The stated relation includes a power-law term in N and an exponential term in compute, rather than a power law in every listed quantity.
rows.check: This is an upper bound derived from Theorem 4.2, not a measured loss. The loss falls exponentially in compute C, not as a power law. The N^-0.25 term comes from bound algebra, not from observation.

rows.subject: 1-bit MLP (depth 3)
rows.operation_detail: Measures minimum training loss while scaling model parameter count.
rows.measure: Minimum quadratic training loss versus parameter count
rows.note: The text says loss decreases as parameter count increases; no numerical loss values or fitted exponent are given.
rows.check: These are training losses on 100 sampled points at three parameter counts, shown only in Fig. 1 with no fit or exponent. A monotone decrease toward ~1e-18 reflects interpolation or optimisation precision, not a power-law scaling form. FP32 rows (r3, r5, ...) are comparators.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical 1-bit two-layer linear-network training loss as a function of parameter count, on the stated dataset setup
reader_labels.reason: Proposition 4.3 gives a term proportional to N^-0.25; row r1 records the stated relation.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toy-function MLP parameter sweeps in Section 6.1
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports decreasing minimum loss with increasing parameter count across the tested targets and depths; rows r2–r25 record those plotted sweeps.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Empirical toy-function MLP results and the compute component of the theoretical relation
reader_labels.reason: The experiments report a downward trend but do not fit or quantify a power law, and Proposition 4.3 gives an exponential compute term rather than a power law in compute; rows r1–r31.
